subject: Maths
topic: Relations and Functions — Inverse and Composition

questions.q: Let f(x) = |x| + x and g(x) = |x| - x for real x. Which description of the two compositions is correct?
options: A) (g o f)(x) = 0 for every real x, while (f o g)(x) = 0 for x >= 0 and -4x for x < 0
B) (f o g)(x) = 0 for every real x, while (g o f)(x) = 0 for x >= 0 and -4x for x < 0
C) Both compositions equal 2x for x >= 0 and -2x for x < 0
D) The two compositions are identical to the identity function on R
questions.answer: A) (g o f)(x) = 0 for every real x, while (f o g)(x) = 0 for x >= 0 and -4x for x < 0
questions.explanation: For x >= 0, f(x)=2x and g(x)=0, so g(f(x))=0 and f(g(x))=0. For x<0, f(x)=0 while g(x)=-2x>0, hence g(f(x))=0 but f(g(x))=2(-2x)=-4x. Therefore the source functions give the first stated piecewise pair of compositions.

questions.q: For f:R->R defined by f(x)=3x-4, which candidate inverse also passes both composition checks f(f^-1(x))=x and f^-1(f(x))=x?
questions.explanation: Set y=3x-4 and solve for x to get x=(y+4)/3, so the inverse candidate is (x+4)/3. Substitution gives f((x+4)/3)=x and f^-1(3x-4)=x. Since both compositions are identity maps, the function is invertible with the stated inverse.

questions.q: Let f:A->B and g:B->C. Suppose g o f is injective and also g o f is surjective. What is forced by these two facts even though the converses of the basic composition results need not hold?
options: A) g must be injective and f must be surjective
B) Both f and g must be bijective
C) f must be injective and g must be surjective
D) Only f must be surjective
questions.answer: C) f must be injective and g must be surjective
questions.explanation: If g o f is one-one, equality f(x1)=f(x2) would force (g o f)(x1)=(g o f)(x2), so x1=x2 and f must be injective. If g o f is onto C, every element of C is hit by g at a value coming from f, so g must be surjective. These conclusions do not by themselves force g to be injective or f to be surjective.

questions.q: On R define a*b=a+b-ab. The identity is 0. Which statement about inverses with respect to * is correct?
options: A) Every real a has inverse -a
B) Every nonzero real a has inverse 1/a
C) Only a=0 has an inverse
D) Every a except 1 has inverse a/(a-1), while a=1 has no inverse
questions.answer: D) Every a except 1 has inverse a/(a-1), while a=1 has no inverse
questions.explanation: An inverse b of a must satisfy a*b=0, so a+b-ab=0. Rearranging gives b(1-a)=-a, hence b=a/(a-1) when a is not 1. For a=1, 1*b=1 for every b, so it can never equal the identity 0.
